item.title: Judge Excludes Key Confession in Sept. 11 Case
item.description:
In a major blow to the U.S. case against Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, the man accused of plotting the Sept. 11 attacks, a military judge ruled on Friday that the prisoner’s confessions to F.B.I. agents were not voluntary and cannot be used against him at trial.

Prosecutors have described Mr. Mohammed’s interrogations in 2007 at the U.S. Navy base in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, as the government’s most crucial evidence in the long-running death-penalty case.

The ruling, just before the 25th anniversary of the attacks, could further delay the start of a trial if prosecutors decide to appeal to reinstate it. Aging survivors and families of victims have said they worry they may never see a final resolution to the case.

Just this week, the judge set a trial date of June 5, 2028.

Mr. Mohammed is accused of being the mastermind of the hijacking attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania and the Pentagon.

He was brutally interrogated by the C.I.A. in secret overseas prisons after his capture in 2003 and held incommunicado until his transfer to Guantánamo in 2006. Prosecutors excluded statements from those interrogations from the case.

But the trial judge, Lt. Col. Michael Schrama, went further, concluding that Mr. Mohammed’s subsequent interrogations in 2007 at Guantánamo were also inadmissible.

“The prosecution has failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Mr. Mohammad’s statements to the F.B.I. were voluntarily given,” Colonel Schrama wrote in the conclusion of his 45-page ruling, which was not immediately released to the public but whose unclassified contents were confirmed by several lawyers who had seen it.

Colonel Schrama cited several factors, including an “unbroken continuation of the C.I.A.’s psychological conditioning and severe coercion” at the time of Mr. Mohammed’s questioning at Guantánamo in 2007.

He also found that F.B.I. agents intentionally failed to explicitly tell Mr. Mohammed that he had a right to be silent and to consult a lawyer, and that what he told them could be used against him at a trial.

The chief prosecutor, Rear Adm. Aaron C. Rugh, said his team would review the ruling “and will make a decision on whether to appeal in the near future.”

The judge gave prosecutors five days to decide but said they could request an additional five days.

The question of the taint of torture has hung over the case for years.

Defense lawyers had argued that Mr. Mohammed was essentially conditioned by the C.I.A. through torture coupled with years of isolation and solitary confinement to later tell the F.B.I. what they wanted to hear. He was not allowed to consult a lawyer until long after he had confessed and was charged.

Colonel Schrama has yet to rule on the confessions of two other defendants in the Sept. 11 case, Walid bin Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi. An earlier judge, Col. Matthew McCall, threw out the confessions of Mr. Mohammed’s nephew, Ammar al-Baluchi, who is accused of helping some of the 19 hijackers with finances and travel arrangements.

A different judge, Col. Lanny Acosta, suppressed the confession of the defendant in the U.S.S. Cole bombing case, Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, in an explicit finding that he had been tortured by the C.I.A. His death-penalty trial in the 2000 attack, which killed 17 U.S. sailors, is scheduled to start in October.

The Sept. 11 case has been mired in pretrial proceedings since arraignment in 2012. Over the years, four other judges gathered evidence on the question Colonel Schrama decided on Friday. An earlier judge found a fifth man, Ramzi bin al-Shibh, mentally incompetent to stand trial, a condition the defendant’s lawyer blamed on torture.

item.title: Tank That Imploded, Killing 11, Was Known to Be Unsafe, Report Says
item.description:
A chemical tank at a paper plant in Washington that imploded and killed 11 people in May was deemed at risk of failure nearly a year before the disaster, according to federal investigators.

In a preliminary report released on Friday, the investigators said that Nippon Dynawave Packaging, the owner of the plant, had hired a private firm to inspect the tank in July 2025.

Inspections that month found “significant thinning” in the walls of G Tank, which held a caustic mixture of sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide.

The inspection firm, which also conducted follow-up inspections in October 2025 and February 2026, recommended that Nippon Dynawave conduct an internal inspection of the tank and make repairs.

But according to the new report from investigators with the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, the company “did not internally inspect G Tank or make any repairs to the tank’s shell between the July 2025 inspection and the May 2026 incident.”

Instead, Nippon Dynawave continued using G tank and did not reduce the amount of liquid stored or the frequency with which the tank was used.

The liquid mixture is used in the process of turning wood chips into bleached paper pulp for packaging such as milk and juice cartons. The 1.2 million-gallon tank was installed in 1987 at the Longview, Wash., plant.

In a note sent to employees on Friday, Nippon Dynawave president’s, Matt Peerboom, said the federal report did not include important context and details about how the company handled plant safety before the disaster. He noted that investigations into workplace accidents like the Longview explosion can take several years and urged patience.

“We hope that all agencies share our commitment to allowing a full investigative process to proceed and establish a complete and accurate record before conclusions are reached,” he wrote. “We will continue to communicate transparently with the investigating regulatory agencies.”

Leaders of the union that represents Nippon Dynawave’s Longview employees said the preliminary report was “deeply troubling” and that the families of victims “deserve a complete accounting” of how and why the tank was still being used.

Kyle Findley, a lawyer representing the family of two brothers who died in the implosion, Tyler and Bradley Covington, promised “to work tirelessly to ensure those responsible for this horrific accident are held accountable and their families receive justice.”

Federal and state investigators are still trying to determine the precise cause of the May 26 implosion. A disruption elsewhere in the plant had driven the level of liquid in the tank to about 90 percent of its capacity when it imploded, according to the federal report.

The tank stood in a courtyard near several maintenance shops, locker rooms and an employee break room. When its walls failed, a wave of white liquor heated to 200 degrees flooded the courtyard, crushing several vehicles and rolling into the lower floors of surrounding buildings.

All 11 workers who died suffered severe chemical burns; one also suffered blunt-force injuries and another died partly from asphyxia.

Federal investigators said Nippon Dynawave’s initial call for emergency assistance from the company’s internal medical team did not warn them that liquid had spilled. One person attempting to rescue a worker in the courtyard waded into the liquid, believing it was water, and suffered serious chemical burns.

Nippon Dynawave employs about 530 people at the plant in Longview, Wash., about 45 minutes north of Portland, Ore., along the Columbia River.

The spill also sent liquid into the plant’s storm water and wastewater systems and nearby drainage ditches of the small city. Some contaminated water bypassed treatment and flowed into the Columbia River, while larger amounts collected in nearby ditches, contributing to widespread fish deaths.

During the cleanup, the local public works department flushed the contaminated ditches with water and pumped the runoff into the river.

Earlier this week, Washington state environmental regulators made an initial determination that Nippon Dynawave Packaging had committed 35 environmental violations related to the spill and its aftermath. The company has 30 days to respond before the state decides whether to impose fines or take other enforcement action.

item.title: $42 Million Abu Ghraib Jury Verdict Is Overturned on Appeal
item.description:
A three-judge appeals panel on Friday overturned a landmark jury verdict that found a Virginia contractor liable for the abuse of three Iraqis detained in 2003 and 2004.

The same panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit had previously upheld the verdict. But that was before the Supreme Court in June set new limits on the federal courts’ jurisdiction over violations of international law.

The Supreme Court’s opinion involved a different matter. But in an unsigned ruling, the appeals court panel wrote that the new precedent “effectively overruled” their previous finding that U.S. courts had jurisdiction over the plaintiffs’ claims through the Alien Tort Statute.

Friday’s decision suggests that one of the longest-running cases on the federal docket could be headed toward a conclusion. During two trials, both held in 2024, jurors heard testimony from the plaintiffs, Salah Hasan Al-Ejaili, a journalist, Suhail Al Shimari, a middle-school principal, and Asa’ad Al-Zuba’e, a fruit vendor.

The three men were arrested after the U.S. invaded Iraq in March of 2003 and took over Abu Ghraib, a prison outside Baghdad used by Saddam Hussein’s government. They were held on a special tier for detainees believed to possess valuable intelligence. According to military officers cited in a Red Cross report, “70 to 90 percent” of Iraqis who were detained by U.S. and allied forces “had been arrested by mistake.”

At the prison, the men said they were subjected to harsh and degrading treatment at the hands of their captors, including threats against family members and being chained to pipes overnight.

The trials marked the first time that civilian jurors had heard accounts of America’s post-9/11 torture program directly from detainees.

The plaintiffs could now file a new lawsuit, appeal to the Supreme Court, or ask the case to be heard again by a larger appellate panel.

The first jury that heard the case was unable to reach a verdict. A second jury awarded each of the men $3 million in compensation and another $11 million in punitive damages.

The money was to be paid by CACI International, a Virginia-based military contractor that supplied interrogators to the U.S. Army at the prison. The jury found that CACI conspired with U.S. soldiers to “inflict torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment” on the three detainees.

“They believed us and sided with us,” said Mr. Al-Ejaili in a statement on Friday. “History will show that it was the Supreme Court that denied us justice.”

Baher Azmy, the legal director of the Center for Constitutional Rights, declined to say whether his clients would pursue further recourse. He called the ruling “a high-level jurisdictional decision,” and added, “it does nothing to wipe away the jury’s conclusion that CACI was responsible for the torture and abuse of men in Abu Ghraib, including our clients.”

A spokesman for CACI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The panel that handed down Friday’s ruling consisted of Judges Henry F. Floyd and Stephanie Thacker, both Obama appointees, and Judge A. Marvin Quattlebaum Jr., a Trump appointee. They instructed the district court judge who oversaw the two trials, Judge Leonie M. Brinkema of the Eastern District of Virginia, to dismiss the case.

The Alien Tort Statute is a 1789 law that gives non-U.S. citizens the right to sue in federal court for some violations of international law. The recent Supreme Court ruling limited its scope to cases where there were violations of the rights of passport holders, “infringement of the rights of ambassadors, and piracy.” In that case, the court ruled that members of the Falun Gong spiritual movement could not sue a U.S. company that they claimed helped facilitate the Chinese government’s efforts to target and torture them.

item.title: Trump Creates a Space Academy and Honors the Artemis Astronauts
item.description:
Declaring that space exploration is “the hot thing,” President Trump on Friday signed an executive order creating a U.S. space academy and presented Medals of Honor to the Artemis II crew, which completed a historic 10-day flight around the moon.

At an event at the NASA Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Mr. Trump presented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the crew’s commander, Reid Wiseman; its pilot, Victor Glover; and the mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen.

In doing so, Mr. Trump carried out the traditional presidential duties of honoring American heroes who united the country with their achievements. He referred to the astronauts as “fearless explorers.”

Mr. Trump also announced that he was signing an executive order to create a U.S. Space Academy to feed the U.S. Space Force and NASA. Few details were released on Mr. Trump’s plans for the academy, but the president indicated they were preliminary and its location had not yet been determined.

The executive order created a commission chaired by the head of NASA tasked with “proposing key details for the establishment of the Space Academy” within 120 days.

“Space is the hot thing,” Mr. Trump told the crowd.

The event also carried a political dimension ahead of the midterm elections. The president’s approval rating is underwater, dragged down by high prices and an unpopular war against Iran, and his party is in danger of losing its control of both chambers of Congress.

Speakers at the event in Houston heaped praise not only on the astronauts, but also on Mr. Trump.

Col. Matt Anderson, the deputy administrator of NASA, told the crowd that “none of this would be possible without strong leadership from the top.”

“President Trump ignited the golden age of exploration and discovery. He gave us the vision,” Mr. Anderson said. “His Working Families Tax Cut Act gave us the resources, and the Artemis II crew took the first steps.”

In April, the Artemis II mission galvanized the country and transfixed the public.

Over 10 days, the astronauts looped around the moon’s far side before returning to Earth, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean. The astronauts saw parts of the moon no human had ever laid eyes on. They broke the record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled from Earth.

The Congressional Space Medal of Honor has been awarded to fewer than three dozen astronauts beginning in the 1970s, according to NASA.

item.title: Autopsy Shows Man Killed by National Guard in Memphis Was Shot in Back
item.description:
An autopsy released this week showed that a man killed by National Guard troops in Memphis in July was shot in the back. The report contradicted initial police reports about the encounter and reignited anger among residents and officials already opposed to the federal task force tackling crime in the city.

Officials had said two Guard members, who were working with the Memphis Safe Task Force, shot the man, Tyrin Johnson, 20, after they joined police officers who were responding to reports of gunfire and chasing him on foot in the early hours of July 5. According to the version of events by law enforcement described in the autopsy, Mr. Johnson was shot once in the chest after he had turned toward law enforcement and pulled a gun.

The autopsy showed the gunshot wound was in Mr. Johnson’s back, and that the bullet exited through his right upper chest. There was no soot or muzzle imprint, indicating that the bullet was not fired close to Mr. Johnson’s body, the report said. The report also noted Mr. Johnson was found with a handgun magazine with rounds.

The autopsy, conducted by the medical examiner at the West Tennessee Regional Forensic Center and shared by a family lawyer, declared Mr. Johnson’s death a homicide.

The findings, first reported by The Commercial Appeal, “reinforce the serious concerns” Mr. Johnson’s family and supporters have about the incident, said André Wharton, a lawyer for the family, in a statement. And it “only further underscores the devastating nature of this encounter.”

Mr. Johnson was one of at least four people killed in altercations with law enforcement working with the Memphis Safe Task Force.

The task force has been in Memphis since last fall, part of a surge of law enforcement sent by the Trump administration to Democratic-led cities. In Memphis, the operation was framed as a crime-fighting initiative where federal, state and local law enforcement all collaborated.

No charges have been filed in the case. A spokesman for the Memphis Safe Task Force declined to comment, citing an ongoing state-led investigation, but said that National Guard patrols were paused as of Friday. It was unclear when they would resume.

Representatives for the Tennessee National Guard did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Memphis task force has been a divisive presence in a majority-Black city that has long struggled with both persistent high rates of crime and discriminatory, heavy-handed policing. Mayor Paul Young, a Democrat, has supported allowing Memphis police officers to work in tandem with federal agents and Tennessee Highway Patrol officers, but he has expressed concerns with National Guard troops supporting the effort.

The task force has made more than 2,000 arrests after Mr. Trump signed an executive order establishing the group in September. Crime has dropped since it took hold, but the task force’s critics have argued that crime had already started to decrease after spiking during the early years of the coronavirus pandemic.

Democratic lawmakers said the autopsy was further evidence that the task force was causing more harm in the city. There is an ongoing lawsuit against leaders of the task force, accusing them of retaliating against residents working to document arrests and detainment of undocumented immigrants.

“I am asking the same question every Memphian is asking: How does a man get shot in the back while allegedly turning toward the people who shot him?” said State Senator Raumesh Akbari, a Democrat. She added, “Memphians want to be safe, but an approach that increases tension and leaves families without straight answers is not public safety — it is a threat to it.”

Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican nominee for governor, is among those who have defended the task force’s presence earlier, including earlier this month on social media.

“The Memphis Safe Task Force is delivering real results, and we have the momentum to make Memphis the safest city in America,” she said.

National Guard troops and federal immigration agents have been pulled back from most other Democratic-led cities, after a flurry of deployments in the first year of the Trump administration. But they have remained in Washington, D.C., where the federal government has outsized power, and Memphis, where Republican leaders have embraced President Trump’s aggressive tactics toward addressing crime.

item.title: The Local: Michael Che on First Avenue
item.description:
Good afternoon! I was up early yesterday to enjoy a breakfast fitting of the State Fair: a key-lime pie ice cream bar. There was a crush of first day, early bird fair visitors at the gate, but despite no clearly demarcated lines, we all generally refrained from cutting and maneuvering. Because we’re Minnesotan.

As I explain to friends elsewhere, “Minnesota Nice” contains a spectrum of connotations, from sarcastic to sincere and every shade in between. At the fair, I got to see the most genuine versions of Minnesota Nice on display. I asked for directions to a restaurant and instead a jovial bunch walked me there because they were kind of, maybe, headed in that direction. That’s the fair at its best.

Today my co-host, Jay Gabler, has a look at the pickled products available at the fair this year. We also chat with Michael Che, the “Saturday Night Live” actor and writer, who is in Minneapolis this weekend to film a live comedy special.

Here’s what else we’ve been following:

Operation Metro Surge is one of the topics that has loomed large among this year’s crop art at the fair. MPR photographer Ben Hovland has a great visual roundup previewing some of the pieces.

The same hyperlocal neighborhood networks that shared information and resources during Metro Surge are now turning to voter organizing, with training and encouragement led by Unidos MN, reports Joey Peters of Sahan Journal.

You’ve noticed it, too: Prices at some food spots in the cities increasingly veer toward the unfathomable. Adam Platt at Twin Cities Business reports why a side salad now costs $15.

Sign up here to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox or share this link with a friend who might like to join us.

The comedian Michael Che is best known for his performances on “Saturday Night Live,” where he is co-host of the news parody segment “Weekend Update.” But his first love, he says, is doing stand-up, and he’s bringing that to Minneapolis this weekend. He’s shooting his third Netflix comedy special, this time at First Avenue, with live shows tonight and tomorrow.

First Avenue, where Prince set “Purple Rain,” is imbued with artistic significance. The club was an incubator of the “Minneapolis Sound” that Prince popularized, and later became a Twin Cities landmark in its own right.

This interview has been lightly edited.

SHADI: Why did you choose First Avenue as the venue for your special?

MICHAEL: I loved how old it is, and how it used to be an old Greyhound station, and just the feeling that the more intimate, historic space gives you.

I liken it to a really good skillet, a really good pan that’s been used for a lot of stews. Each one leaves a little bit of flavor in there. You sense that vibe when you walk in, where you can feel the music still in the walls.

Why did you want to film stand-up in front of a Twin Cities audience?

Certain cities receive shows well. They’re there to see something, and they’re on board. You don’t have to fight them. You can tell they’ve been outside before, you know.

Maybe part of it is Minneapolis’s remarkable theater background. Audiences there get performance, and you can see that by how many artists, musicians, performers come from there. It’s a breeding ground for talent, so they’re used to shows and they just dig it.

I’ll also be in Minneapolis to finally solve the mystery of who really invented the Juicy Lucy.

Did the federal immigration surge affect your decision to come here?

This is the first I’m hearing about it. Did something happen here?

Of course there’s a cultural significance to being around people who are on the front lines of any fight for social change. I always loved performing with them and for them because they matched my frustration about having to prove our humanity to anyone. That’s where a lot of my performance, my humor, comes from, and it matches the spirit of Minneapolis.

This particular night, I want people to let their energy out through laughter. That doesn’t discount other ways of processing it. But I handle things best through jokes. And you’ve got to use your superpower.

It’s Jay here. Minnesotans might be loath to admit it, but the association of pickles with state fairs reaches beyond our borders. Competitive pickling figures prominently in Rodgers and Hammerstein’s “State Fair,” although the Iowans in that 1945 musical modestly claim only that “our state fair is the best state fair in our state.”

At the best state fair in our own state, pickles are pervasive.

Official competitions include 13 pickle categories, including six for cucumbers alone. Refrigerator pickles need not apply.

Outside the competitions, the taste of pickle pervades the fair. Pickle items include:

Fried pickles. While I would make a case for the spear as the ideal fried pickle cut (try an order at the Groveland Tap), at the State Fair it’s all about the rounds. The Perfect Pickle’s two locations offer multiple fried pickle varieties, thickly breaded.

Pickle pizza. A surprise hit (to me) when it debuted in 2022, the weighty slices at Rick’s Pizza go way beyond the topping. The sauce is dill ranch, the seasoning is dill weed. Short of sticking a slice into a jar of brine, you can’t get pizza much more pickled than this.

Pickle booze. If you’re looking to get pickled in multiple senses of the word, your options include beer (Dill Pickle Kölsch), cider (Pickle Lemonade Cider), seltzer (Dill Pickle Seltzer) and even sparkling wine (Pickle & Vine). If hard liquor were allowed at the fair, a pickle-tini would be inevitable.

Pickle dog. Have you ever looked at a tray of pickle roll-ups and thought, “What if we just didn’t slice them?” The result would be a pickle dog: a quarter dill snuggled up in a slice of pastrami with a cream cheese buffer.

New pickle frontiers. This year’s new food list includes both a Pickle Pie (LuLu’s Public House) and a pickle cookie (“Dill with it, Cookie!” at Urban Glow Mocktails). Shadi’s take on the Pickle Pie, one of this year’s most talked-about new foods: “Prepare yourself for something really pickle-y.”

Pickle on a stick. The classic, available at the Pickle Dog stand and the Perfect Pickle. Consider it a palate cleanser.

Want to learn more about pickles? Wirecutter, The Times’s product recommendation site, will be at MPR’s booth at the State Fair for a live podcast recording on Sunday, Aug. 30, at noon. The subject: pickles.

We’ll be back at the fair this weekend — watch for Jay’s report from Saturday’s Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis Homecoming show. Here are a few more weekend recommendations.

Shania Twain has become a cultural icon (don’t miss Lizzy Goodman’s recent article in The New York Times Magazine). An annual Twain tribute at the Turf Club reliably brings some of the Twin Cities’ most exciting singers to the stage, and Saturday’s show will be no exception.

After five years as an online publication, Racket hits print this weekend. Friday night at Arbeiter Brewing, Racket will be celebrating its anniversary as well as the release of a book containing eight stories from its virtual pages. Ross Raihala at Pioneer Press has the story of Racket’s rise.

The Guthrie Theater’s 2006 move was the key to a transformation that’s completely changed the vibe of the Mill District. Sunday, the Guthrie is marking two decades with an open house free to the public.

There may be extra anxiety among parents as football season begins for Minnesota high school students.

A new study, which we referenced in an earlier newsletter, found that among the nearly 900 former N.F.L. players who died from 2016 to 2021, at least one in four had C.T.E., or chronic traumatic encephalopathy. The neurological disease, which causes dementia-like symptoms, impulsivity and depression, has also been found in children as young as 15.

So what should you do if your children play tackle football?

Researchers advise looking for ways to minimize the total number of blows to the head. Limit contact in practice, and be wary of coaches or teams that have a “play through it” mentality. If your child is knocked unconscious, they should be removed from the game and evaluated by an independent medical professional before returning to the field.

Football is among the most popular sports among high school students in Minnesota. After reaching a low point during the 2021-2022 school year, participation among Minnesotan students rose and now remains fairly steady. During the last school year, 23,816 Minnesota athletes played football, according to data from the National Federation of State High School Associations.

Top Times stories, selected for Minnesota readers. We have made these links free for readers of The Local.

Big Tech: Tech companies like Google, Microsoft and Apple have influenced nearly every step of the education supply chain. St. Paul public schools rely on iPads, and Minneapolis public schools use Chromebooks.

Deportation flights: The Trump administration is planning to expand deportation flights to Haiti, according to documents obtained by The New York Times. In mid-August, a federal judge also ruled that the Trump administration could end Temporary Protective Status for people from Somalia.

Divorce: Divorcées in Minnesota and elsewhere are choosing to celebrate their new life status with indulgence, big hats, long dresses and, maybe, empowerment.

Heat can deter people from visiting the State Fair, according to an Axios Twin Cities analysis, but rain? Not so much. That suggests crowds tomorrow will still be sizable despite the strong possibility of a midday thunderstorm. Today, gathering cloud cover will make an expected 85 degree high feel more bearable.

No sooner had we decided to embrace “ope” than Shadi spotted this tattoo on a fair-goer.

Thanks for taking a break with us this afternoon!

Sign up here if you don’t already get this newsletter delivered to your inbox.

Are you on WhatsApp? Join us there, too, to keep up with us between sends.

Feedback? Questions? We’d love to hear from you: thelocalTC@nytimes.com

item.title: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Uphold Ban on Transgender Troops
item.description:
The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow the U.S. military to fully enforce its ban on transgender service members, setting up the latest test of the administration’s policy priorities in front of the court.

The justices are expected to consider whether to review the legality of the administration’s ban this fall and, if they accept the case, could schedule oral arguments during the Supreme Court’s term that begins in October.

A few days after returning to office, Mr. Trump issued an executive order banning all trans troops and characterizing transgender identity as a “falsehood” that “conflicts with a soldier’s commitment to an honorable, truthful and disciplined lifestyle.”

The ban was one of a series of actions by the administration targeting transgender rights. The president also directed government agencies to withdraw federal funding from schools that allow transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports.

The Defense Department implemented Mr. Trump’s military order in February 2025, effectively forcing trans troops out of the military.

“No more dudes in dresses,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced then.

Transgender service members quickly sued. About 4,200 openly transgender people were in the military last year, according to government court filings — about 0.1 percent of the armed forces. They worked as infantry platoon leaders, pilots, nuclear engineers, doctors, intelligence analysts, police and other key professionals.

A series of lower-court rulings have protected a group of transgender troops who challenged the ban from being discharged while litigation continued. But last May, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority agreed in a separate case to generally allow the administration to dismiss troops while litigation continued.

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, urged the justices in a filing on Thursday to reverse the lower courts on a permanent basis and defer to the nation’s military leaders by upholding the Defense Department’s “considered military judgment” that accommodating trans troops would undermine “military effectiveness and lethality.”

“The authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance,” he wrote, pushing back on lower-court rulings that said the administration’s policy was discriminatory.

In the past year, many transgender service members have left the military voluntarily rather than face uncertainty and possible harm by contesting the new policy. Hundreds of others have stayed, insisting that their cases be considered individually by military retention boards consisting of fellow service members. Discharge has generally been a foregone conclusion, given the president’s order.

The 28 challengers in the case before the justices are led by Nicolas Talbott, a second lieutenant in the U.S. Army Reserve. The group claims the policy unfairly and illegally directs hostility and prejudice against a group of people.

In a 2-to-1 decision in June, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sided with the group, but their lawyers have asked a lower court to extend protections to all transgender troops.

The policy seemed to be “driven by the bare desire to harm a politically unpopular group,” wrote Judge Robert L. Wilkins, who was joined by Judge Judith W. Rogers.

Judge Justin R. Walker dissented, saying courts do not have the power to make such decisions about the military: “The Constitution assigns that authority to Congress and the commander in chief,” he wrote.

In the meantime, the 28 service members have been in limbo, still technically in the military but on leave, according to their lawyers.

Attorneys for the service members urged the justices on Friday to deny the administration’s request and allow the case to first go to trial in January. The service members are meeting the military’s standards and the government should not “kick out thousands of highly trained, skilled and decorated troops based on nothing but hostility,” Jennifer Levi, GLAD Law’s senior director of transgender and queer rights, said in a statement.

When the Supreme Court first dealt with the issue on an emergency basis last May, the majority did not explain its reasoning, as is common when the court issues emergency orders. The court’s three liberal justices — Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson — said they would have kept Trump’s policy on hold.

In his first term, Mr. Trump also announced a transgender ban, but two federal judges blocked the policy.

The Supreme Court lifted those injunctions in 2019 by a 5-to-4 vote, allowing a revised ban to take effect while legal challenges moved forward. The cases were dropped after Mr. Trump left office, and President Joseph R. Biden Jr. rescinded the ban.

item.title: Trump Administration Looks to Give a Swath of Yosemite to Developer
item.description:
The Trump administration has proposed trading away a small parcel of land in Yosemite National Park in California so a private developer can gain access to the park, according to federal officials and documents reviewed by The New York Times.

The potential deal has alarmed conservationists and former National Park Service officials, who say that Yosemite, the crown jewel of the nation’s park system, should be off limits to development.

The proposal, details of which were first reported by the news outlet NOTUS, calls for transferring a small parcel just inside the western boundary of Yosemite to a company controlled by Kingsbarn Realty Capital, a real-estate private equity firm. Kingsbarn wants to build a road and develop two 40-acre parcels it owns near the park, according to documents submitted to Congress this year and reviewed by The Times.

In exchange, the company would purchase land of equivalent value, either near Yosemite or elsewhere in California, and hand it over to the Park Service, the documents show.

“This is so ridiculous, it makes you sick,” said Don Neubacher, a former supervisor at Yosemite who is now on the executive council of the nonprofit Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks. Mr. Neubacher said a similar proposal had been raised in the early 2000s. It was rejected, first by the Park Service and later in court.

Kingsbarn bought the two parcels near the park in early 2024 for $4 million through a limited liability corporation called Sanctuary at Yosemite, property records show. The chief executive of Kingsbarn, Jeff Pori, made regular small-dollar donations to President Trump’s 2024 campaign, contributing more than $4,000, according to campaign finance records.

Representatives for Kingsbarn did not respond to a request for comment.

Aubrie Spady, a spokeswoman for the Interior Department, the parent agency of the Park Service, said in a statement that no final decision had been made.

“Any land exchange or access proposal involving National Park Service lands would be subject to all applicable federal laws, regulations and departmental policies, including required environmental review and public notification processes,” Ms. Spady said.

Yosemite is known for its enormous waterfalls, towering sequoias and glacier-carved monoliths like Half Dome and El Capitan. It is one of the country’s most visited national parks, and it has been even more crowded than usual after the Trump administration eliminated a summer reservation system.

Political appointees at the Interior Department have discussed the proposed land exchange in Yosemite for more than a year, calling it a top priority, according to two former Park Service officials who asked to remain anonymous because they feared retaliation.

The Interior Department notified Congress this year that it was considering paying for any costs related to the exchange via the Land and Water Conservation Fund. That drew criticism from Democrats, who said the fund was intended to pay for conservation programs on public lands.

California’s two Democratic senators, Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, both decried the proposal and said they were working with the Senate Appropriations Committee to try to block it.

“This is the most corrupt administration in history,” Mr. Padilla said in a statement. “The Land and Water Conservation Fund exists to acquire land and interests in land in order to safeguard natural areas, water resources and cultural heritage — and to provide recreation opportunities for all Americans.”

Cicely Muldoon, who was the superintendent of Yosemite from 2020 until her retirement in February 2025, said that land exchanges were supposed to provide the Park Service with a net benefit, such as additional wildlife habitat. She said the benefit of this one for the public was unclear.

Ms. Muldoon also raised concern about the precedent the deal could set for more than 400 other national parks and historic sites around the country.

“Yosemite is kind of a bellwether for the national parks,” she said. “If this can happen in Yosemite, it can really happen anywhere in the national park system.”

The land at issue has been embroiled in development disputes since the late 1990s, when Lewis Geyser, a developer from Solvang, Calif., purchased a rugged stretch of forest on Yosemite’s western border and proposed building a resort called Hazel Green Ranch.

The proposed project was near the Big Oak Flat entrance to Yosemite on California State Route 120. Initially, park officials sought to work with the owner to create an off-site lot so that visitors could leave their cars outside Yosemite and take a shuttle into the park grounds. That plan fell apart.

Mr. Geyser then sought an easement through a quarter-mile section of park property that would provide easier access to the park from his land, according to court records in the long litigation that followed.

After the park refused, he sued in 2007. The Sierra Club and other environmental groups joined the federal government in opposing the easement, and the litigation dragged out until 2012, when a federal appeals court in San Francisco ruled against the developer.

“It was a good ending, and we all thought it was dead,” said Mr. Neubacher, who was the superintendent at Yosemite from 2010 until 2016. “Yosemite is a spectacular cathedral, but if it is to be preserved for future generations, we can’t just keep packing cars on the road.”

After Kingsbarn bought the land in 2024, however, the firm sought to reopen discussions about a private road and was told that the Park Service could not legally permit the access, Ms. Muldoon said.

Then Mr. Trump took office again.

By spring 2025, the department was revisiting the request from Kingsbarn, according to current and former federal officials with knowledge of the conversations, and word circulated that the proposal was a priority for political appointees in Washington, D.C.

item.title: Trump Administration Appeals Ruling Halting Mail-In Voting Rules
item.description:
The Trump administration on Friday appealed a freeze on President Trump’s plan to restrict mail-in voting, teeing up another series of legal decisions about whether the U.S. Postal Service can make changes to how ballots are handled ahead of the midterm elections.

The issue will likely be settled by the Supreme Court.

The administration’s appeal came less than a day after a federal judge in Massachusetts found that a Postal Service rule published last week was likely unconstitutional and exceeded the agency’s authority. Under the rule, the Postal Service would not deliver mail ballots in states that do not share voter data with the agency, and would only deliver ballots that meet certain criteria.

The Supreme Court has considered the issue once already, finding that it was too soon for litigants to challenge an executive order issued by Mr. Trump in March because the Postal Service had not yet taken steps to carry it out.

But after the Postal Service published its plan last week, more than 20 Democratic state attorneys general and a coalition of voting nonprofits and organizations returned to court with a more concrete challenge.

The Trump administration had argued that the Postal Service plan would not give the agency an overly intrusive role scrutinizing voters or regulating election mail.

“The Postal Service will not determine voter eligibility, ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures,” the agency said in a filing.

In a ruling on Thursday, Judge Indira Talwani of the Federal District Court for the District of Massachusetts wrote that while the Supreme Court had previously said the issue was not ripe, the justices had also concluded that it was not yet clear if the administration’s plan was lawful. She wrote that it was likely not.

item.title: It’s Trump’s Capital Now, but Voters Aren’t Living in It
item.description:
For nearly his entire second term, President Trump has worked to transform the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington into a reflection of himself, with his name on the front. The takeover has driven off 100 percent of its paid performances, 90 percent of its employees and hundreds of millions of dollars in private donations, cratering the center’s finances.

The newly politicized Kennedy Center has become an empty shell with more mice than people. As the damage mounted, Trump announced plans to close the center for a renovation. But this week, his administration’s lawyers escalated a legal fight over whether to keep his name on the empty building, raising the possibility of demolishing the place if he doesn’t get his way.

Trump has just over two months before midterm elections that could profoundly reshape what’s left of his presidency, and he has a lot on his plate, including a war with Iran and a skittish economy. Yet my colleague Maggie Haberman told me that he continues to spend the bulk of his working hours on changes to the Kennedy Center and the Smithsonian, a new White House ballroom, the botched Reflecting Pool remodel, a new “Garden of Heroes” sculpture park, an enormous triumphal arch and assorted gilded gewgaws.

These capital projects could cost well over a billion dollars, at significant taxpayer expense, despite White House claims to the contrary.

I’ve been writing about the president’s attacks on the Kennedy Center for months. Tonight, I ask: How does his preoccupation with remaking Washington’s landmarks play outside the capital?

Like plenty of conservative or moderate Americans, Trump believes the nation’s cultural institutions have swung too far to the left, but unlike many Americans, he views his personal redesign of the capital’s institutions and landmarks as a priority.

In a poll last month, CNN asked voters whether they thought Trump had gone too far, not far enough, or had been about right when it came to making changes to cultural institutions like the Kennedy Center and the Smithsonian. Perhaps predictably, 84 percent of Democrats said he had gone too far, while only 28 percent of Republicans agreed.

Among independents, who could be crucial in the midterms, 63 percent said Trump had gone too far.

Capital construction projects were also unpopular. Asked whether Trump had gone too far in remodeling the White House and other Washington landmarks, 86 percent of Democrats, 29 percent of Republicans and 64 percent of independents agreed.

The same poll made clear that voters felt more strongly about other issues, including the economy and Trump’s personal business gains while in office, like the $2.2 billion or more he pulled in on crypto and other ventures last year.

Asked whether Trump had gone too far when it came to pursuing his personal business interests while serving as president, 71 percent of independents agreed, as did 91 percent of Democrats and nearly a quarter of Republicans.

With all of his focus on gilding statues, painting and repainting the Reflecting Pool, and scoping out a fancy new golf course on the Potomac, Trump could be sending a dissonant signal to Americans at a key moment for his party.

“He was re-elected to do four things: bring down inflation, juice the economy, stop illegal immigration and get away from woke culture,” Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist, told me. Voters are giving him “very poor marks thus far on the first two,” he added. The message: “Voters care a lot more about what happens in their lives than what happens in his life.”

Democrats have pointed to Trump’s remodeling habit as evidence that “he doesn’t want to do the job,” as Senator Jon Ossoff, Democrat of Georgia, put it this month: “He wants to build his ballroom.”

Over the past 15 months Trump “has squandered what was always his superpower — people had more trust in him on the economy than they had in him as a person,” Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist, told me. In the midterms, he said, Democrats’ core indictment of Republican decision-making is that the party is ignoring voters’ concerns, as exemplified by a president “who knows the price of marble but doesn’t know the price of milk.”

Fewer than one-quarter of independents in the CNN poll agreed that Trump had placed the good of the country above his personal gain; 82 percent of independents said he hadn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important problems.

Those problems include the cost of gas, groceries, housing and health care. Voters broadly disapprove of Trump’s handling of the economy and the war with Iran.

Not on their list of priorities: whether or not his name adorns the Kennedy Center.

Ruth Igielnik contributed reporting.

My colleagues Tim Balk, Shane Goldmacher and Maggie Haberman explain how Republicans are caught in a bind when it comes to Trump, the midterms and the uncertainty about his money.

In One Graphic

At first glance, Trump appears to have a knack for selecting successful primary candidates, including Senator Darline Graham, who narrowly prevailed in South Carolina this week.

item.title: Milo Yiannopoulos, a Right-Wing Provocateur, Is Arrested by ICE
item.description:
The Trump administration said on Friday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers had arrested Milo Yiannopoulos, the prominent right-wing agitator and early supporter of President Trump, at the New Orleans airport.

Public ICE detention records confirmed that Mr. Yiannopoulos was in custody, but did not say where he was being held. The Homeland Security Department said that Mr. Yiannopoulos had overstayed his visa and was issued a final deportation order in July. That order means Mr. Yiannopoulos faces possible removal from the country.

The Homeland Security Department publicized Mr. Yiannopoulos’s arrest, circulating an unflattering mug shot and warning other immigrants to “take control of their departure” by self-deporting.

The arrest follows the Trump administration’s efforts targeting foreign citizens as they travel through airports, a tactic that opened a vast pool of people for deportation. Immigration agents in plain clothes have in recent months whisked away targets at check-in counters and arrival gates with the help of information provided by airlines to the Transportation Security Administration.

Mr. Yiannopoulos is a British citizen who has lived in the United States since 2015, when he entered the country to join the staff of Breitbart News using a nonimmigrant visa reserved for people with “extraordinary ability.” He did not respond to messages seeking comment.

Mr. Yiannopoulos was a prominent supporter of Donald J. Trump during his 2016 run for president. In addition to his work at Breitbart, Mr. Yiannopoulos was briefly offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, a pre-eminent platform for the American right, in 2017.

But Mr. Yiannopoulos abruptly fell from grace after the publication of a video in which he condoned sexual relations with boys as young as 13 and laughed off the seriousness of pedophilia by Roman Catholic priests. The organizers of CPAC rescinded their invitation, and he resigned from Breitbart under scrutiny for his remarks.

An acid-tongued provocateur who is no stranger to controversy, Mr. Yiannopoulos was banned from the site then known as Twitter in 2016 for leading a harassment campaign against a Black actress. His account was reinstated in 2022 by Elon Musk, who purchased the platform and later renamed it X.

More recently, Mr. Yiannopoulos made headlines for serving as a temporary staffer for Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Republican representative, and for working for the fashion brand of Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West.

In 2022 he claimed credit for organizing a notorious dinner for Mr. Trump and Mr. West that also included the white supremacist Nick Fuentes. (Mr. Yiannopoulos claimed the meeting was an ambush, meant to “make Trump’s life miserable.”) Two years later, Mr. Yiannopoulos joined Mr. West’s exploratory campaign for president.

Mr. Yiannopoulos, who was openly gay and often said he was attracted to Mr. Trump, announced in 2017 that he had been married to a man who is a U.S. citizen, but never revealed the full identity of that person. He later claimed that he was “ex-gay,” and had “demoted” his husband to the role of “housemate.”

He has been a particular target of Laura Loomer, the right-wing activist who frequently speaks to Mr. Trump. The two were once close allies, with Mr. Yiannopoulos supporting her unsuccessful run for Congress in 2020, but had a public falling out.

Since late 2024, Ms. Loomer has been calling for him to be deported, claiming that he was in the country on an expired visa.

In a phone call on Friday, Ms. Loomer took credit for the arrest, saying that she had long ago notified Department of Homeland Security of potential issues with Mr. Yiannopoulos’s immigration status.

“Loomered!” she said, using a term she applies to the growing collection of people who have been fired, deported or otherwise reprimanded by the Trump administration after her specific calls for action. “I have been saying this should happen for a long time and now it did.”

Other prominent figures on the right were quick to celebrate the news. “Deport immediately,” Enrique Tarrio, the former leader of the Proud Boys, wrote on X. “Good riddance.”

Mr. Yiannopoulos himself had reveled in Mr. Trump’s mass deportations, calling for ICE checkpoints at supermarkets and gas stations and “total legal immunity for ICE agents when they’re on duty.”

item.title: California Sues Trump Administration Over Offshore Wind Cancellation
item.description:
In the latest salvo in California’s ongoing environmental battle with the White House, the state on Friday sued the Trump administration over its attempt to kill offshore wind farms.

Mr. Trump has long despised offshore wind power, falsely saying that it does not work and kills whales. This spring, his administration struck deals with energy companies. In exchange for refunds for what they paid for offshore wind leases, the companies agreed to use the money on oil and gas projects.

One of the deals involved a company called Golden State Wind, which was in the early stages of building a floating wind farm near Morro Bay, along California’s Central Coast. Under the agreement, the U.S. Department of the Interior said it would return $120 million the company had paid for the offshore lease in 2022, to be used on fossil-fuel projects.

Rob Bonta, the state attorney general, and the California Energy Commission on Friday sued the Trump administration and Golden State Wind, saying their agreement to forgo the wind farm jeopardized thousands of jobs and the state’s investments in the offshore wind industry.

Mr. Bonta called the deal a “backroom buyout” by the Trump administration that was intended to “line the pockets” of “Big Oil donors.”

The White House declined to comment on California’s lawsuit. A spokesperson for the Interior Department said that California had been throwing “good money at bad ideas” and that the settlements with the energy companies were voluntary and had been reviewed by the Department of Justice.

“This administration will not sit back and let reckless projects create higher utility costs, a weakened energy system and unnecessary harm to the environment,” a representative with the department wrote in an email.

Golden State Wind did not return a request for comment.

David Hochschild, chair of the California Energy Commission, said that California would continue to focus on clean energy as a way to reduce pollution and provide new jobs.

“We will not let the Trump administration’s reckless actions turn back the clock,” he said in a statement. “California’s clean energy future is worth fighting for. See you in court.”

item.title: Hegseth Blocks Promotions of Four Army Officers as Purge Widens
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is blocking the promotions of four Army officers selected for promotion to one-star rank, a highly unusual move that appears to be targeting officers who worked for generals he does not like, current and former defense officials said.

So far this year Mr. Hegseth has removed at least 45 officers, selected by boards made up of peers, from promotion lists. More than half of those officers have been female or Black.

Mr. Hegseth’s actions appear to violate the rules governing a promotion system that is meant to be apolitical and merit-based.

Some of the Army officers pulled from the latest list appear to have worked recently for Gen. Randy George, the former Army chief of staff, whom Mr. Hegseth fired without explanation in April. The others have ties to Gen. Christopher T. Donahue, the top U.S. Army commander in Europe, who was forced to leave the Army this summer, defense officials said.

Typically, Army one-star promotion lists consist of about three dozen officers.

General George and General Donahue led the Army’s push to adapt to a future battlefield dominated by drones and artificial intelligence and the officers pulled from the recent lists played important roles in shaping their modernization vision.

An officer whose promotion was blocked commanded one of the Army’s first “transformation in contact” brigades, officials said. These 3,000-soldier units were encouraged to experiment with new drone and artificial intelligence technology, even as they trained for war.

The officer developed a new formation that use drones, electronic warfare systems and traditional scouts to see and strike the enemy deep behind the front lines. His idea was adopted by all of the Army’s infantry brigades.

The officer was also targeted, in part, because of an essay he wrote in a graduate program on the implications of political polarization on the Army’s ability to recruit and retain talent, said officials familiar with the list. It is unclear why Mr. Hegseth or members of his team found the essay objectionable.

“Military promotions are given to those who have earned them,” Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, said in a statement. “This has always been the case under Secretary Hegseth and will not change.”

In March, Mr. Hegseth struck four officers from an Army one-star promotion list that had consisted of 34 officers. Two of the officers targeted by Mr. Hegseth were Black men and two were women, prompting some senior military officials to question whether the officers were singled out because of their race or gender.

Beyond the blocking of officers for promotion to one-star rank and the firing of General George, Mr. Hegseth has fired or forced out a half-dozen senior officers — a generation of the Army’s most combat-hardened leaders — thinning the service’s top ranks for the next several years, officials said.

The personnel turmoil has also left a vacuum at the top of the Army at a moment when it is responsible for defending troops against the threat posed by cheap drones and missiles.

The Army has not had a chief of staff, the service’s top officer, since Mr. Hegseth fired General George in April, and there are no signs that he is close to filling the position, said current and former officials. Mr. Hegseth’s choice to take over as Army chief, Gen. Christopher LaNeve, does not currently have enough support in the Senate to be confirmed, officials said.

General LaNeve, who previously served as Mr. Hegseth’s senior military aide, has expressed frustration with Mr. Hegseth’s decision to block qualified officers for promotions and is concerned this will dilute the Army’s pool of experienced leaders, defense officials said.

Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll, the service’s top civilian leader, could leave the administration as soon as next week, officials said. Mr. Hegseth has indicated that he would like to nominate Mr. Parnell to take over for Mr. Driscoll.

Mr. Parnell served as an officer in Afghanistan, but his tenure as the Pentagon’s chief spokesman has been buffeted by controversy. Mr. Parnell recently fired three journalists at Stars and Stripes, a federally funded but independent news organization. The journalists sued the government on Thursday, claiming that the Pentagon fired them in retaliation for writing about the worsening conditions on a Navy aircraft carrier deployed to the Middle East.

Mr. Parnell also led an effort to restrict reporters’ access within the Pentagon. The moves prompted The New York Times to sue the Pentagon on the grounds that the policy violated the First Amendment.

Mr. Parnell withdrew from a Senate race in November 2021 after a judge ruled that his estranged wife should have primary custody of their three children in a case in which she accused him of spousal and child abuse. Mr. Hegseth’s interest in nominating Mr. Parnell was first reported by The Hill.

White House officials are concerned that if Mr. Driscoll leaves that Mr. Parnell will not be able to garner enough Senate votes for confirmation, leaving the Army’s top civilian and uniform military jobs open.

Many of the senior Army officers fired or forced out by Mr. Hegseth gathered Thursday at Fort Bragg, N.C., for General Donahue’s retirement ceremony. The tone at the gathering was somber — one former military official in attendance described it as a “state funeral.”

In what could be one of his last acts as Army secretary, Mr. Driscoll joined the fired officers, all of them combat-tested leaders who had been groomed to lead the Army. Together they said goodbye to General Donahue.

item.title: James Roche, Embattled Air Force Secretary, Dies at 86
item.description:
James G. Roche, who was secretary of the Air Force during an uproar over sexual assault at the Air Force Academy and a multibillion-dollar procurement scandal — twin controversies that prematurely ended his career as a rising star at the Pentagon in the early 2000s — died on Aug. 4 at his home in Annapolis, Md. He was 86.

The cause was vascular disease, Bill Bodie, a former Pentagon aide to Mr. Roche, said.

Mr. Roche served in the Navy for 23 years before retiring with the rank of captain in 1983. Later, as a senior executive at Northrop Corporation, which designed the B-2 Stealth bomber, he helped guide the company’s 1994 purchase of Grumman Aerospace, creating the defense contracting giant Northrop Grumman.

In the private sector, Mr. Roche was known for his innovative leadership. At Northrop Grumman, he brought in consultants to oversee a daylong Shakespeare workshop, during which he donned a cardboard crown and blue robe to declaim Henry V’s famous rallying cry at the siege of Harfleur: “The game’s afoot.”

He became a favorite of Defense Secretary Donald H. Rumsfeld and President George W. Bush, who nominated him as Air Force secretary in April 2001 in the hope of bringing corporate discipline to the Pentagon bureaucracy.

As Air Force secretary, Mr. Roche sought to contain the Air Force Academy scandal, which erupted in early 2003. Several current and former female cadets disclosed that they had been ignored or punished for reporting that they had been raped or sexually abused.

A report in The New York Times suggested that as many as half of the female cadets at the academy had experienced rape or sexual assault, but most chose not to report it for fear of reprisals in the toxic male culture of the academy, which did not begin admitting women until 1976.

In a speech in late February 2003 at the academy in Colorado Springs, Mr. Roche castigated students for tolerating sexual assault, while acknowledging that decade-old protocols to prevent rape had failed. He also replaced the top four officers at the academy and assembled an Air Force panel to review the allegations.

The panel largely defended the academy in a June 2003 report, asserting that its leaders had not mishandled complaints. It went on make some recommendations that were considered tone-deaf: offering first-year female cadets assertiveness training and removing a motto above a stone arch that read, “Bring Me Men.”

A congressional panel reviewing the assaults was much harsher, placing blame on the top Air Force leadership. “Since at least 1993,” the independent investigation found in a report released that September, “the highest levels of Air Force leadership have known of serious sexual misconduct problems at the academy,” but failed to respond effectively.

The commission praised some steps that Mr. Roche laid out, but said that they did “not go far enough.”

The scandal did not immediately tarnish Mr. Roche in the eyes of the Bush administration. The president nominated him to be secretary of the Army in May 2003, another high-level appointment. But his candidacy was soon overshadowed by his role in supporting a major deal with the Boeing Company.

The Air Force proposed to lease 100 of Boeing’s 767 aircraft and retrofit them as midair refueling tankers. But it soon emerged that the No. 2 weapons buyer for the Air Force, a civilian official who promoted the deal, was steering contracts to Boeing while seeking a $250,000 job at the company. She and a Boeing executive eventually went to prison.

Mr. Roche, who was not linked to a criminal scheme, was also an avid supporter of the $23 billion tanker deal. The deal fell apart under congressional opposition, in particular from Senator John S. McCain, Republican of Arizona. From his perch on the Committee on Armed Services, Mr. McCain accused the Air Force of wasting taxpayer money.

Mr. McCain was so incensed that he put a hold on Mr. Roche’s nomination for Army secretary. The White House, recognizing political reality, withdrew the nomination in March 2024. Mr. Roche announced his resignation as Air Force secretary that November, a few days before Mr. McCain released emails that showed Mr. Roche had been a cheerleader for Boeing, writing, “Go Boeing!” and criticizing opponents of the tanker deal as “fools.”

James Gerard Roche was born on Dec. 16, 1939, in Brooklyn, to Gerald Roche, a machinist, and Elizabeth (Counihan) Roche.

He received a humanities degree from the Illinois Institute of Technology in Chicago in 1960, the same year that he was commissioned as an ensign in the Navy and married Diane Mikula.

During the Vietnam War, Mr. Roche led search-and-rescue missions in the Gulf of Tonkin. He went on to command the U.S.S. Buchanan, a guided missile destroyer, in 1973-74.

While on active duty, he earned a master’s degree in operations research in 1966 from the Naval Postgraduate School in Monterey, Calif., and a doctorate of business administration from Harvard Business School in 1972. He held jobs at the Pentagon during the Ford and Carter administrations.

After retiring from the Navy, Mr. Roche briefly served as Democratic staff director for the Senate Committee on Armed Services before joining Northrop. He advised the company’s chief executive on a strategy to survive post-Cold War cuts to military weapons by acquiring other businesses, and the newly formed Northrop Grumman went on a buying spree.

“He had a diversification strategy in the mid-90s that turned the company around,” Mr. Bodie, who worked as an aide to Mr. Roche in the private sector before following him to the Pentagon, said in an interview.

Mr. Roche’s wife died in January. He is survived by a daughter, Heather Roche. His son, Sean, died in 1987.

Mr. Roche brought his experience as a leadership guru in the private sector to the Air Force, hiring the same corporate consultants to teach Shakespeare to the generals. Even after he stepped down as secretary, he remained interested in the seminars, and in January 2005 he visited one on “Julius Caesar” in which generals debated the assassination of the Roman dictator.

“People can talk about some things more easily when they do it in the context of the play,” Mr. Roche explained to The Times, which reported on the exercise. “So when I became secretary, I suggested we try it with our officers.”

item.title: For Trump, the Iran War Is Stuck Between Combat and Genuine Peace
item.description:
President Trump the other day posted a heroic image of himself backed by an aircraft carrier, warplanes and American flags. In the lower left corner was former President George W. Bush and a sign, “Mission Not Accomplished 2001-2021.” In the other corner was a sign referencing himself saying “Mission Accomplished 2026.”

Except that it is not. Mr. Trump’s war in Iran, which hit the six-month mark on Friday, is anything but accomplished. Half a year in, the conflict has deteriorated into a quagmire of the president’s own making with no clear goals, no obvious strategy and no end in sight. Mr. Trump, who came to power running against Mr. Bush’s “forever wars,” has staked his presidency on his own version.

For Mr. Trump, it may be the worst of both worlds. He finds himself stuck in a maddening purgatory between full-fledged combat and genuine peace. He is reluctant to resume an all-out bombardment despite his thunderous threats, yet has been unable so far to broker an agreement to end the war on satisfactory terms. He has no victory to take credit for, yet is paying the political price in terms of the toll on the American economy and his party’s chances in the fall elections.

This sort of in-between stasis could in theory extend for a long time, a far cry from the four-to-six-week lightning strike that Mr. Trump predicted when he ordered Operation Epic Fury at the end of February. With no breakthrough in sight, both sides are testing the other’s staying power and Mr. Trump, despite a history of impatience, has made clear that he is “not in a hurry,” as he put it earlier this week.

“There’s not a lot to speak to,” he told reporters on Thursday, disavowing interest in negotiating with Iran at this point. “We don’t want to speak to them; we’re not looking to meet or anything. The strait is open; we’re taking a lot of boats — millions and millions of barrels of oil are coming out of the strait every day.”

In fact, the Strait of Hormuz remains a volatile passage with only a fraction of its prewar shipping traffic, leaving oil markets in flux. While the war killed Iran’s supreme leader, he was replaced by his son and the brutal regime in charge six months ago remains in charge today. Iran’s nuclear program has been damaged but Tehran still refuses to give it up.

“This has been a fiasco,” said Richard N. Haass, who was director of policy planning at the State Department when Mr. Bush invaded Iraq in 2003. “That’s the harsh reality. He can declare ‘mission accomplished.’ He can try to sell the argument as he often tries to, almost to create reality. But it’s going to be a hard, hard sell. There’s nothing to point to that will suggest either that we are better off or that the war was worth it.”

Supporters of the war have counseled forbearance, arguing that Mr. Trump has succeeded in substantially weakening a radical and dangerous Iran with far fewer American casualties than during Mr. Bush’s ground wars in Iraq or Afghanistan. If Mr. Trump sticks with it, they said, he may yet force Iran to back down through military force or economic pressure, making America safer in the long run.

“I know this cuts against the conventional wisdom, but I believe President Trump is winning the confrontation with the regime in Iran,” said Mark Dubowitz, chief executive of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “The Islamic Republic has never been weaker in its 47-year history. And it was forced to play its most important card — the Strait of Hormuz — from a position of extraordinary weakness.”

Mr. Dubowitz said that Iran now is left deciding whether to negotiate seriously or spend the next two years under relentless pressure. “We are not at peace, and we aren’t in major combat operations,” he said. “President Trump may instead have found the strategic sweet spot between the two: sustained coercive pressure without either a major war or an unacceptable agreement.”

However it turns out, the war in Iran has become arguably the biggest gamble of Mr. Trump’s presidency, at least in foreign policy, and a case study in how he has approached his second term differently than his first.

While his original four years in power were defined by a more inward-looking America First policy in reaction to Bush interventionism, Mr. Trump returned to the White House last year more willing to wield power overseas and seemingly more intent on reshaping the world to his liking.

His decapitation of Venezuela’s leadership, his threats to take over Greenland, the Panama Canal and Cuba, even his renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America this week all speak to a legacy-minded president looking to leave his mark beyond U.S. borders. Any hopes that Iran would be a quick and decisive success, however, have long since been dispelled and now the main aim is how to find a way out that can be framed as a victory of some sort.

“It strikes me that Operation Epic Fury is quintessentially Trump,” said Steven A. Cook, a longtime Middle East scholar at the Council on Foreign Relations. “It is no doubt bold, but its orchestrator is mostly careless and unprepared, prosecuting a conflict on the seat of his pants and a lot of bluster.”

Mr. Cook added: “The U.S. could win in the end, but it would only be because it is powerful despite Trump’s mistakes and the Iranians are relatively weak, not because the president pursued an effective strategy.”

Victor Davis Hanson, a senior fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution, disagreed, saying that Mr. Trump is pursuing what he called “an anaconda Civil War strategy” that will eventually pay off.

“He’s going to squeeze them as much as he can, and as they start to pop, they will send off missiles or drones from their vestigial fleet, and he’ll hit them hard,” he said in a Daily Signal podcast this week. “And he hopes that will continue, that containment will continue to the midterms.”

Mr. Hanson added that the economic pressure on Iran could ultimately generate popular uprisings or further depress the country’s capacity. “Is that victory? I don’t know,” he said. But he added that it could stop Iran from developing a nuclear weapon at a cost in lives and treasure far below Mr. Bush’s wars. “Take that versus a trillion dollars in Iraq and probably $2 trillion in Afghanistan over 20 years,” he said.

Putting aside dollars and cents, the story of Mr. Trump’s war in its first six months can be told in five numbers: Sixty-three, 12, 1.10, 18 and 759. The first measures public opposition to the war. Just 31 percent support it, while 63 percent are against it, according to the latest Ipsos survey, the kind of figures reminiscent of the darkest days of the Vietnam War.

The second reflects the number of ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz each day, averaging about 12, compared with 130 before the war. The third reflects the average price of gas in the United States, which is about $4.09 a gallon, or $1.10 higher than it was at the start of fighting.

The fourth reflects the 18 American military personnel killed so far in the war. And the fifth is the estimated number of Patriot interceptors left in U.S. arsenal, down from 2,330 to as low as 759 a month ago, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a nonpartisan think tank.

As for the goals that Mr. Trump outlined at the start, most remain unmet. He likes to boast that he has destroyed Iran’s air force and navy, but Tehran remains capable of firing at U.S. bases and allies in the region. The day of liberation he forecast for the Iranian people throwing off their oppressors never arrived. Iran’s ability to support proxy terrorist groups in the region has been diminished but not eliminated. And its nuclear program has been seriously damaged but the regime refuses to abandon it and could reconstitute it, according to analysts.

“President Trump has entangled the United States in a foreign policy failure of historic consequence,” Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said in a statement on Friday. “Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved. Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly.”

Mr. Haass, who was skeptical of Mr. Bush’s plan to invade Iraq while working in his administration and later wrote a book about its failure called “War of Necessity, War of Choice,” said that paradoxically both that conflict and Mr. Trump’s have left Iran stronger.

In the case of Iraq, Iran became a dominant force inside its next-door enemy after Saddam Hussein was toppled, Mr. Haass noted, and now Iran has demonstrated its ability to roil world energy markets by choking off shipping through the strait. “Iran is the strategic beneficiary of both wars,” he said.

Mr. Trump, of course, would dispute that. In fact, he has argued time and again that he has already prevailed against Iran. “We’ve already won,” he declared on March 7, barely a week into the war. “We won everything; we have all the cards,” he said on April 25. “We’ve already won that,” he said on May 4. “I don’t know if you heard, but we ended the war with Iran today,” he said on June 11, celebrating a cease-fire that did not last.

His “Mission Accomplished” social media post this week was a play off Mr. Bush’s own ill-fated speech in front of a banner with those words aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier just weeks after the original Iraq invasion in 2003, a pronouncement that later was taken as a metaphor for premature declaration of victory. If Mr. Trump saw the irony in invoking it himself, he did not indicate it, but many others did.

“Trump is clearly wrong to say the U.S. has won,” said Brett H. McGurk, a longtime Middle East adviser for presidents of both parties, including Mr. Bush, Barack Obama, Mr. Trump in his first term and finally Joseph R. Biden Jr. “Few of its stated aims have been met. But Iran has not won either.”

Mr. McGurk, who was a key architect of Mr. Bush’s second-term military surge and strategy shift in Iraq that helped turn the war around, said that experience showed that even a president in his final two years in office can have an impact. And he noted that Mr. Trump seems more committed to seeing the Iran war through than many had presumed.

“Six months is a blip in the Middle East,” Mr. McGurk said. “This war, like many, will not have a clean endpoint. It will merely shift advantage in an ongoing contest. And it’s too early to call where average ultimately settles.”
